title: The sugar is still there
body: Sugar is made of particles, tiny bits far too small to see. Stir it into water, and the water pulls those bits off one by one. They spread out between the bits of water. Soon they are too small and too spread out to see.

Nothing gets destroyed. Every bit of sugar is still in the beaker. It's like a friend walking into a huge crowd. You can't spot them, but they're still there. So the sugar water weighs exactly as much as the water and sugar did before.
Water can only take so much, though. At room temperature, 1 g of water can dissolve about 2 g of sugar. Add more than that, and the extra stays as grains at the bottom.
equation: sugar water on the scale = water + sugar
realWorld: Seawater looks clear, but every litre hides about 35 g of salt. Leave it out in the sun and the water dries up. The salt stays behind, and that's how sea salt is made.
sources: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, §1.2 Phases and Classification of Matter. https://openstax.org/books/chemistry-2e/pages/1-2-phases-and-classification-of-matter
